prompt: Drag both poles straight up, away from the real axis. What happens to the overshoot, and why?

tryFirst.nudge: Try it first: drag a pole straight up in the s-plane and watch the step response while you do.

points.hint: Look at the highest point of the curve while you drag up. Does it climb or drop?

points.found: And it oscillates faster: the imaginary part is the damped frequency.
points.hint: Also watch the wiggles after the peak. Do they come closer together or further apart?

points.found: The reason: moving away from the real axis widens the angle θ, so the damping ratio ζ = cos θ drops, and lower ζ means more overshoot.
points.hint: For the why, watch the damping ratio readout and the dashed line from the origin to the pole.

misconceptions.reply: Check the settling-time readout, though: it hardly moves. Going straight up keeps the real part fixed, and the real part sets how fast the response settles.
Careful with ζ: watch its readout while you drag up. It goes down, not up.

followUp: Now try the other direction: move both poles straight left. What changes this time, and what stays the same?
